The nonsurgical management of osteoarthritis is among the most challenging of topics
to learn as an orthopaedic surgeon. Orthopaedic surgeons chose orthopaedic surgery
and the topic of nonsurgical management of musculoskeletal conditions does not always
create the most excitement for surgeons. However, nonsurgical management of
osteoarthritis is one of the most important topics that a practicing orthopaedic surgeon
will have to master because it critically integrates the practice and art of medicine.
Nonarthroplasty management of osteoarthritis includes some surgical treatment
options that may aim to salvage or prolong the life of the native joint via arthroscopy,
osteotomy, or other means; however, for most patients with osteoarthritis,
nonarthroplasty treatment often equates with nonsurgical treatment.
Osteoarthritis of the Knee
Osteoarthritis of the knee is common, and more than 85% of individuals older than 65 years
have radiographically detectable osteoarthritis.
Osteoarthritis of the knee is multifactorial, associated with increased age and obesity, and may
result from primary or secondary causes.
Knowledge of how to manage osteoarthritis of the knee is important for multiple reasons.

Osteoarthritis of the Knee
Osteoarthritis of the knee is a degenerative condition that leads to pain, stiffness, and
disability. The condition is quite common, with estimates of 25% to 30% of individuals
aged 45 to 64 years and more than 85% of individuals older than 65 years having
radiographically detectable osteoarthritis.1,2 Osteoarthritis of the knee may result from
primary causes or idiopathic wear and tear degeneration. Uncertainty exists with regard
to whether primary osteoarthritis is related to activity, genetics, or other causes.3
Secondary osteoarthritis of the knee causes include inflammatory arthritis, structural or
alignment derangements, and posttraumatic causes. In some patients, prior surgical
treatment may lead to accelerated osteoarthritic changes.4 Increased age and body
mass index are directly correlated with osteoarthritis of the knee.1 Obesity, which is
increasingly common in the population, is concomitant in approximately 66% of

individuals with osteoarthritis of the knee. Ultimately, osteoarthritis of the knee is a
multifactorial disease that is influenced by age, sex, family history, heritable
predispositions, race, injury, and lifestyle.
In addition to the successful treatment of some patients with knee osteoarthritis to
improve pain and function without surgery, another important reason to master this
topic is to appropriately select patients who will ultimately require arthroplasty. To
perform surgery, surgeons first must appropriately identify patients who are suitable
candidates surgery. One risk factor that persists, despite optimization of modifiable
medical conditions, is the appropriateness of the patient and his or her disease for
surgical treatment because not all patients are suitable candidates for surgery. In the
knee arthroplasty literature, the incidence of patients dissatisfied after knee
replacement is as high as 20%.1 In addition, studies have shown that patients with less
severe arthritis tend to experience a higher incidence of dissatisfaction. The importance
of identifying and appropriately treating patients via evidence-based nonsurgical
treatment measures is important to avoid performing surgery in patients who may not
have a good outcome or who have less severity of disease and should not undergo
arthroplasty. The incidence of osteoarthritis is increasing as the population ages. The
population also is staying more active into later years in life and has higher demands and
expectations to continue those high levels of activity. Therefore, knowledge of and
appropriate use of nonarthroplasty management of osteoarthritis of the knee in
appropriate patients will become increasingly important.
Nonarthroplasty Management
The nonarthroplasty management of osteoarthritis of the knee includes surgical and
nonsurgical options.
No cure for osteoarthritis of the knee exists; however, most treatment options aim to prolong
the native joint and delay arthroplasty via medical or surgical treatment options that aim to
decrease pain and improve function.


Nonarthroplasty Management
Total knee arthroplasty may be indicated for optimized and ideal candidates who have
advanced osteoarthritis unresponsive to nonsurgical management; however, not all
patients with osteoarthritis of the knee ultimately require arthroplasty. Despite
considerable sentiment among the general public, a diagnosis of arthritis does not
equate to unavoidable arthroplasty. If a patient has adequate symptom relief that allows
them to perform the activities that they need to do (activities of daily living, work, self-
care, care for their family, care for their home, and exercise) and want to do (activities of
leisure or recreation), then nonarthroplasty treatment options may be beneficial. In
addition, some patterns of arthritis remain structurally stable over the long term,
whereas others patterns lead to erosive or destructive changes. Obviously, the former
often is more amenable to prolonged nonarthroplasty management than the latter.
Despite the major advances in science and modern medicine, the mainstays of
nonarthroplasty management of osteoarthritis focus on symptom management, pain
alleviation, and preservation of function rather than slowing,, correcting, or reversing the
damage. Proven, effective, and durable treatment options to reverse or cure
osteoarthritis do not exist. This is the case for nonsurgical treatment options, with the
goal of most treatment options being to address and alleviate pain. Although
nonarthroplasty surgical treatment options, such as osteotomies, chondrocyte
implantation; osteoarticular grafting; meniscal transplantation; and biologic nonsurgical
treatment options, such as stem cell injections and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections,
may alleviate pain, they do not restore cartilage damage that already has occurred.
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-Based
Clinical Practice Guideline
The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) Evidence-Based Clinical Practice
Guideline (CPG) on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee is a source for the most
relevant review of data and evidence-based guidance on nonarthroplasty management of
knee osteoarthritis (Resources 1 and 2).

American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-Based Clinical
Practice Guideline
In 2008, 2013, and 2021, the AAOS published an evidence-based CPG on best
recommendations for the nonsurgical management of osteoarthritis of the knee (the 15
recommendations are summarized in Table 1).5-8 The AAOS recommends strengthening
exercises, low-impact aerobic exercises, aquatic exercises, weight loss programs, and
NSAIDs; however, they did not identify conclusive evidence to guide recommendations
on other common treatment options, such as knee bracing, intra-articular corticosteroid
injections (CSIs), or acetaminophen or pain medications.9 Although the exhaustive
literature review in the guideline provides some of the best available evidence to guide
management of osteoarthritis of the knee to date, the publication was not without
controversy, and complete use and widespread adoption of many of the
recommendations are lacking.5

One of the most controversial recommendations was that of strong evidence against the
use of viscosupplementation and hyaluronic acid injections, which had been a highly
used treatment modality in the years prior to the publication of the CPG. The major
controversies surrounding this particular recommendation included the already limited
number of tools in the tool chest to manage osteoarthritis of the knee, the effect it had
on reimbursement of management, and the conflicting evidence in the literature.10 Not
only did the recommendation against use of the intervention alarm some providers but
the option also was essentially eliminated from their tool chest because many insurers
and payers quickly stopped reimbursing for the rather expensive viscosupplementation
therapy. Although the AAOS literature review did not find evidence to support the use of
viscosupplementation, not all professional societies agreed. For example, highlighting
the importance of focusing on the outcomes of individual patients within trials, the
American Medical Society for Sports Medicine released their review of the literature and
recommended the use of hyaluronic acid injection in appropriate patients with
osteoarthritis of the knee.11
The AAOS Evidence-Based CPG on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee is one of
the most comprehensive literature reviews to date that provide recommendations and
guidance to patients and providers for the management of osteoarthritis of the knee.
Although not without some controversy and although medical treatment should be
based on clinical evidence and physician judgment and patient wishes, the ongoing
review of pertinent literature and the establishment of this CPG is a crucial step toward
identifying and providing the most effective treatment options for the management of
osteoarthritis of the knee.
Nonsurgical Management
In general, the goals of these therapeutic options are to decrease pain and improve function.

Some of these modalities also may have a disease-modifying effect by altering the mechanical
environment of the knee.
Appropriate selection and successful implementation of nonsurgical treatment modalities
requires knowledge of the literature, careful patient selection, patient education, and
adequate follow-up.
Weight Loss
Weight loss is a safe and effective method to improve knee pain, function, and stiffness
without serious adverse effects; however, weight loss may be a challenge for patients with
obesity who have osteoarthritis of the knee because of limited mobility, limited resources, and
lack of adherence to a low-calorie diet.
Providing education and offering tangible resources to patients may result in better
compliance with weight loss recommendations.

Weight Loss
Obesity commonly is associated with osteoarthritis of the knee. Whether obesity is
modifiable can be argued. Obesity may contribute to osteoarthritis of the knee in various
ways other than just increased stress and forces across the joint, including potential
endocrine and inflammatory cytokine pathways; therefore, the benefits of obesity
management may extend beyond the mechanical advantages of reducing loads at the
joint.12,13 With little risk or disadvantages, weight loss has been shown to be effective in
improving pain, function, and stiffness and reduces the risk for symptomatic
osteoarthritis of the knee.14-22 Although weight loss and exercise potentially are
beneficial interventions to aid in reducing weight and stress on osteoarthritic joints,
many patients will report that joint pain prevents them from exercising and losing
weight. Expecting patients to lose weight without providing education about their
options is unrealistic. In addition, providing patients with resources to help them, such
as that which may be available at a comprehensive multidisciplinary medical weight loss
clinic, has been shown to improve engagement and outcomes.23

Physical Therapy and Exercise
Studies have shown that exercise, with focus on aerobic conditioning and muscle
strengthening, can reduce pain and improve function despite the presence of osteoarthritis of
the knee.
Formal physical therapy also may be beneficial and may be required by some payers if a
patient ultimately requires total knee arthroplasty; however, considerable variability exists in
outcomes and treatment options being evaluated.

Physical Therapy and Exercise
Randomized controlled trials have shown that exercise can reduce pain and improve
function in patients with early osteoarthritis.24-26 The most effective programs appear to
be those that include muscle strengthening and aerobic exercise via a home program
and supervised exercise classes.26,27 Low-impact exercises, including cycling and
swimming, offer advantages of less load across the joint while allowing for increased
aerobic conditions, range of motion, and muscle strengthening. Antigravity treadmills
are available in some physical therapy centers and gyms and may be of benefit to
patients with osteoarthritis of the knee.28,29 If the exercise program is terminated,
advantages appear to have a minimal lasting effect, suggesting that adherence to and
maintenance of the program are important.25
Although exercise programs are of potential benefit, formal physical therapy does not
necessarily include exercise alone. Many payers require documentation of medical
necessity by demonstrating exhaustion of certain nonsurgical treatment options to
manage osteoarthritis, including supervised exercise or formal physical therapy, before
authorizing a patient to undergo surgical treatment options.30 Although considerable
research has been performed on the role of formal physical therapy, the outcomes of
studies rarely are standardized and the definition of physical therapy vary. Meta-
analyses have shown that the exercise and weight loss components of physical therapy
appear to offer the most benefit, and lower-strength evidence shows that some
modalities performed as part of physical therapy also may offer some benefit.31,32

Bracing
Knee brace options include over-the-counter compression wraps, sleeves, and hinged braces,
among others.
Spring-loaded unloader braces also may be used in some patients with isolated compartment
disease in a correctable deformity.
Long-term brace compliance does not appear to be good.

Bracing
Braces frequently are used by many patients in the general population for many knee
ailments, and many over-the-counter options are available. Knee braces may include
simple compression wraps or sleeves, neoprene, and hinged options. Anecdotally,
patients often report that these devices are helpful; however, little evidence is available
to support their use.
For patients seeking additional advice on the nonsurgical management of knee
osteoarthritis, another type of brace that may be considered is an unloader brace. These
braces, available in off-the-shelf and custom-fit options, likely are most appropriate for
the management of symptomatic unicompartmental arthritis or patients with symptoms
that are predominately on one side of the knee. An unloader braces attempt to change
the load on the involved compartment by placing an asymmetric spring-loaded force to
pull toward the convex side or push open on the concave side of the sagittal deformity.
Ideal candidates for unloader bracing have symptomatic degenerative joint disease
primarily confined to the medial or lateral compartment, have a thin body habitus, and
have passively correctable varus or valgus alignment noted on physical examination. The

NSAIDs
NSAIDs may improve inflammation and pain associated with osteoarthritis of the knee.
Although often well tolerated, concerns exist with regard to gastrointestinal, cardiac, and renal
adverse effects with prolonged NSAID use.

NSAIDs
Oral medications, including NSAIDs, often are used or prescribed to help reduce pain
and inflammation. Selective cyclo-oxygenase-2 inhibitors and nonselective NSAIDs have
been shown to be effective in multiple studies, and the AAOS Evidence-Based CPG on the
Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee includes a strong recommendation in support
for the use of these modalities for the management of symptomatic osteoarthritis of the
knee. Currently, no strong data support one type or class of NSAID over another, and
much of the decision is based on patient factors, preferences, individual efficacy
differences, patient tolerance, adverse effect profiles, safety, and cost.40 Selective cyclo-
oxygenase-2 inhibitors may have improved gastrointestinal tolerance;41 however, all
NSAIDs are associated with some risk of gastrointestinal intolerance or cardiac or renal
adverse effects and should be used with caution.
Pain Medications
Pain medications may include acetaminophen, tramadol, or opioid narcotic agents.
Changes in dosing and variable outcomes have made strong recommendations on the use of
pain medications difficult.
Avoiding the use of opioid narcotic agents for the management of osteoarthritis should be
attempted.

Acetaminophen and tramadol are associated with lower adverse effect profiles and may be
effective at reducing pain associated with osteoarthritis of the knee.

Pain Medications
Pain medications, including acetaminophen, tramadol, and narcotic agents, are potential
options for attempting to control pain associated with osteoarthritis of the knee. The
mechanism of action of these medications is different than that of NSAIDs and does little
to address the inflammation component of arthritis but, instead, attempts to work at the
pain receptors of the body. Interestingly, little is known about the mechanism of action
of one of the most commonly used pain medications, acetaminophen; however, recent
research suggests that it may act on the body’s endogenous cannabinoid receptors.42,43
Available over the counter, occasionally with a commercially available arthritis labeling,
acetaminophen frequently is used by patients to manage pain. The most recent AAOS
Evidence-Based CPG on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee recommendation on
acetaminophen was downgraded from level B (moderate) in the 2008 edition to
inconclusive in the 2013 edition because only one study that was included compared it
against placebo44 and because most prior studies were based on a maximum dosing of
4,000 mg of acetaminophen per day, which recently has been down-adjusted to a
maximum of 3,000 mg for over-the-counter patient use. Therefore, the AAOS Evidence-
Based CPG on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee could not provide adequate
evidence to support its use. Regardless, practitioners and patients often will turn to
acetaminophen as a front-line option for the management of pain related to arthritis
because of its favorable adverse effect profile and ease of use.
Other pain medications, including narcotic agents, also are used to manage pain related
to arthritis. With one of the goals of the management of osteoarthritis of the knee being
to reduce pain, pain medications should be considered; however, considerable adverse
effect profiles, issues of dependence and addiction, systemic alterations, and other
factors make opioid options less than ideal. Tramadol is included in the AAOS Evidence-
Based CPG on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee because its efficacy was
demonstrated in several outcomes in high-quality studies. Although it is associated with
demonstrated efficacy and is not a true opioid, tramadol, which has monoaminergic

Opioids have not been shown to be more effective than nonopioid treatment options,

osteoarthritis.48 However, the prescription of opioids remains common, and ongoing

resulted in considerable changes in this trend; therefore, require ongoing educational
initiatives may be necessary.49
Intra-articular Viscosupplementation
Viscosupplementation with hyaluronic acid may be effective in patients cases; however, data
are variable, and additional rigorous studies are necessary to demonstrate efficacy.

Intra-articular Viscosupplementation
Intra-articular viscosupplementation via hyaluronic acid was a common nonsurgical
treatment option for the management of osteoarthritis of the knee before the
publication of the 2013 AAOS Evidence-Based CPG on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of
the Knee. The mechanism of action is not fully understood but may be imparted by its
mechanical viscoelastic properties and its anti-inflammatory, anabolic, analgesic, and
chondroprotective properties.50 Hyaluronic acid injections may be most effective in
patients with more mild osteoarthritis of the knee, particularly before bone-on-bone
changes occur. Although rare, a unique adverse effect associated with substantial clinical
concern is the pseudoseptic reaction to these injections.51
The AAOS Evidence-Based CPG on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee showed
strong evidence against the use of viscosupplementation and hyaluronic acid injections
based on the body of high-quality evidence published because of lack of uniform patient

Intra-articular CSIs
Intra-articular CSIs have been a mainstay in the management of osteoarthritis of the knee and
currently remain among the most common treatment options offered in practice by providers.
The potential for infectious and noninfectious complications exist with CSIs.
The efficacy of CSIs for the management of OA of the knee remains a subject of controversy;
however, it may be associated with short-term benefits.
Newer, extended-release compounds have shown some promising early results in a few
studies; however, longer-term, high-quality follow-up is necessary.

Intra-articular CSIs
By delivering medication directly to the inflamed joint, the pain relief from a CSI is
thought to work by reducing inflammation. With potentially fewer adverse effects than
oral steroids or NSAIDs for reducing inflammation, the safety of delivering the
medication to the joint appears attractive. Some adverse effects can occur with CSI,
including local reactions, infection, chondrocyte toxicity, and transient elevation of blood
glucose level, which may be problematic in patients with diabetes mellitus.53 Lasting
effects, with potentially increased risk of postoperative infection after subsequent
surgical management, are another concern in terms of safety.54 Rapid progression of
disease is another potential outcome and is poorly understood; however, it should be
considered in the decision-making process.55
The efficacy of CSIs remains a subject of controversy. At best, some short-term benefits
may be afforded to patients with mild to moderate osteoarthritis of the knee; however,
the literature is fraught with a lack of standardization on formulations and types of

The success of steroid injections in relieving arthritic knee pain most often is short term.
The 2013 AAOS Evidence-Based CPG on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee
updated their recommendation to inconclusive evidence to support the use of CSI for
the management of osteoarthritis of the knee, whereas the prior 2008 edition suggested
that CSI may be used for short-term pain relief for patients (a grade of recommendation

If CSI is used, the avoidance of complications and the highest likelihood of efficacy
should be considered. Triamcinolone may offer a potentially longer-lasting effect
because of its lower solubility than other options.56 Although all local anesthetic agents
appear to be associated with some risk of chondrotoxicity, especially with indwelling
catheters, single-dose administration has fewer clear effects, which likely is a time and
dose dependency issue. Despite the single-dose administration, studies have shown that
ropivacaine, at concentrations less than 0.5%, is associated with less chondrotoxicity
than other commonly used local anesthetic agents, including lidocaine and
bupivacaine.57
Newer generations of intra-articular corticosteroids recently have been introduced to the
market. Triamcinolone acetonide extended-release is formulated in poly(lactic-co-glycolic
acid) microspheres that aim to slowly release triamcinolone acetonide, enabling
prolonged presence in the joint.58 Although exciting prospects of longer duration of
effect and potentially lower immediate systemic adverse effects, such as hyperglycemia,
may result from the extended-release formulation, additional high-quality studies are
necessary before widespread adoption and use.
Genicular Nerve Ablation
Several sensory genicular nerves innervate the knee and surrounding tissues.
A potential treatment option to manage pain in the knee associated with osteoarthritis may be
heat- or cooling-based ablation treatment options targeted at the location of those nerves.

Several studies have demonstrated the efficacy of this treatment option; however, given the
lack of standardization with regard to the nerves to treat, long-term outcomes, patients who
may be the best candidates, and the technologies to use for the ablation, additional research
is necessary in future studies.

Genicular Nerve Ablation
More than 10 nerves provide sensory innervation to the anterior knee capsule.
Considerable variability exists in the location of these nerves, and debate exists with
regard to the ideal target locations for genicular ablation. In addition, heated and cooling
radiofrequency ablation treatment options are being used, and outcomes may be
further observed with mixing the outcomes of the management of osteoarthritis with
the management of refractory pain after total knee arthroplasty, which may
demonstrate more variable results.59,60 Despite these factors, favorable outcomes have
been observed in studies targeting the superior medial genicular nerve, inferior medial
genicular nerve, and superior lateral genicular nerve.
Several randomized controlled trials demonstrated superiority of genicular
radiofrequency ablation compared with intra-articular steroids, viscosupplementation,
and oral analgesic agents.59 Although complications are rare in the literature, they
include limited reports of septic arthritis, periarticular hematoma, tendon injury, and
skin burn. Compared with the adverse event profile of other common treatment options
for the management of osteoarthritis of the knee, including cardiovascular,
gastrointestinal, and renal problems with NSAIDs and accelerated cartilage loss and
periprosthetic infection risk with intra-articular CSIs, the safety of genicular
radiofrequency ablation appears acceptable. Although genicular radiofrequency ablation
appears to be effective, additional large-scale, non–industry-sponsored trials are
necessary to provide greater confidence in this potentially beneficial treatment option.
Biologics
The use of stem cells and PRP to manage osteoarthritis of the knee is a subject of controversy.

PRP and stem cells have been used in the management of osteoarthritis of the knee.
Stem cells can be autologous or allogeneic, depending on the source tissue.
PRP and stem cells can be used as injections or as adjuncts to surgical treatment options
(Resource 3).
Autologous stem cell injections have been studied for injection treatment in osteoarthritis of
the knee.
A comparative study showed similar outcomes to a placebo after stem cell injection. 
PRP is obtained by harvesting and centrifuging peripheral blood.
Leukocyte-poor PRP may be better suited for intra-articular use.
The role of PRP in the management of osteoarthritis of the knee continues to be investigated.

Biologics
Recently, interest in the use of biologics in the nonsurgical treatment of patients with
symptomatic osteoarthritis OA of the knee has increased. Studies have been performed
to evaluate the utility of these treatment options in patients with osteoarthritis of the
knee; however, they generally lack midterm and long-term follow-up. The two most
employed biologics in the management of osteoarthritis OA of the knee are PRP and
stem cells. Stem cells can be divided into autologous or allogeneic based on their source
tissue. Commonly used autologous stem cells are harvested from adult adipose tissue or
bone marrow. Allogeneic stem cells may be from placental or amniotic tissues. PRP and
stem cells have been administered via injection and used as adjuncts to cartilage

The concept of microfracture surgery for isolated cartilage defects was introduced in the
1990s and continues to be used today. Biologically, perforation of the subchondral bone
releases marrow elements, including mesenchymal stem cells, which may lead to
fibrocartilage healing of the defect but not replacement with true hyaline cartilage.
Microfracture generally is considered for isolated, smaller (<2 to 3 cm2) defects.
Contraindications include diffuse cartilage damage and so-called kissing lesions involving
the femur and tibia.75 A systematic review of microfracture patients by Mithoefer et al76
showed improved knee function scores for as long as 24 months postoperatively. After
24 months, 47% to 80% of patients had a decline in function. By nature, fibrocartilage is
less durable than native hyaline cartilage; therefore, this decrease in function over time
is not surprising (Figure 2).

OAT is a single-stage procedure in which articular cartilage plugs, including subchondral

substantial improvement in symptoms and early (<6 months) return to sport in patients
with a lesion smaller than 2 cm2.79 In a meta-analysis comparing OAT with microfracture

improved outcomes with ACI, OAT is used in patients with smaller cartilage lesions.

Conclusions
Nonarthroplasty management of symptomatic osteoarthritis of the knee remains an
important consideration for orthopaedic surgeons. The 2013 AAOS Evidence-Based CPG
on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee provides guidance for nonsurgical and
surgical management of osteoarthritis of the knee and is a good primary source for
recommendations. The goal of nonsurgical management is to alleviate pain and afford
improved function. Surgical treatment options may afford decreased symptoms, return
to activity, and knee joint preservation. Cartilage restoration surgery may be an option
for patients with isolated cartilage lesions but is not an option for patients with diffuse or
advanced arthritis. Future directions of nonarthroplasty surgical treatment likely will
include the use of biologics as adjuncts to cartilage restoration surgery. Ultimately, knee
arthroplasty is the best treatment option for patients with symptomatic osteoarthritis in
whom nonsurgical treatment options fail and who have been appropriately selected and
optimized.
